title: Hosea 10:1–8
context: Hosea 10:1–8 pictures Israel as a luxuriant vine whose prosperity only multiplied altars and sacred stones. Their heart is divided, and the LORD will tear down their altars. The people will say they have no king because they did not fear the LORD, and they make empty covenants, so judgment springs up like poisonous weeds. Samaria’s people and priests will mourn over the calf of Beth Aven, a mocking name for Bethel meaning house of wickedness, when the idol is carried to Assyria as tribute to a great king. Samaria’s king will float away like a twig on water, the high places will be overgrown with thorns, and the people will say to the mountains, "Cover us!" and to the hills, "Fall on us!" Jesus uses similar words in Luke 23:30, and they appear again in Revelation 6:16. Throughout, Hosea describes what the LORD will do. Shared ground: both traditions read the unit as a warning that blessing used for idolatry turns into judgment.

verses.text: Israel is a luxuriant vine that produces his fruit. According to the abundance of his fruit he has multiplied his altars. As their land has prospered, they have adorned their sacred stones.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says Israel is a luxuriant vine, but as it prospered it multiplied altars and adorned sacred stones. Arminian readers see blessing turned to idolatry, as the people used God’s gifts for false worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the vine image used elsewhere for Israel (compare Isaiah 5:1–7 and Psalm 80:8–16). Both traditions hold this as shared ground: prosperity can lead people away from God.

verses.text: Their heart is divided. Now they will be found guilty. He will demolish their altars. He will destroy their sacred stones.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says their heart is divided, they will be found guilty, and God will tear down their altars. Arminians see divided loyalty as the core of Israel’s sin, trying to serve the LORD and Baal at once.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the divided heart as the root problem. Both traditions compare the call for an undivided heart elsewhere in Scripture (Psalm 86:11), and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: Surely now they will say, “We have no king; for we don’t fear the LORD; and the king, what can he do for us?”
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says they will say they have no king because they did not fear the LORD, and ask what a king could do for them. Arminian readers see the people realizing too late that their kings could not save them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the futility of trusting human rulers. Both traditions note the political turmoil of Israel’s final years, and they read the verse as anticipating the end of the northern monarchy.

verses.text: They make promises, swearing falsely in making covenants. Therefore judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of the field.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says they make empty promises and false covenants, so judgment springs up like poisonous weeds. Arminians see broken oaths and false agreements leading to justice turned to poison.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing a society without integrity. Both traditions read the image of weeds in a furrow as showing how injustice spreads.

verses.text: The inhabitants of Samaria will be in terror for the calves of Beth Aven, for its people will mourn over it, along with its priests who rejoiced over it, for its glory, because it has departed from it.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says Samaria will fear for the calves of Beth Aven, and its people and priests will mourn when its glory departs. Arminian readers see the people grieving over an idol that could not protect them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the irony of mourning a false god. Both traditions note that Beth Aven, meaning house of wickedness, is Hosea’s mocking name for Bethel, house of God.

verses.text: It also will be carried to Assyria for a present to a great king. Ephraim will receive shame, and Israel will be ashamed of his own counsel.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says the calf will be carried to Assyria as a gift to a great king, and Ephraim will be ashamed of its counsel. Arminians see the idol itself taken away as tribute, exposing its powerlessness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see shame as the result of trusting in idols. Both traditions note that the great king may be a title for the Assyrian ruler, and they hold the exact phrase loosely.

verses.text: Samaria and her king float away like a twig on the water.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says Samaria and its king will float away like a twig on water. Arminian readers see the helplessness of the king before God’s judgment, carried off with no power to resist.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as showing the end of Israel’s monarchy. Both traditions note that some read the twig as foam, and they agree on the picture of something swept away.

verses.text: The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, will be destroyed. The thorn and the thistle will come up on their altars. They will tell the mountains, “Cover us!” and the hills, “Fall on us!”
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says the high places of Aven will be destroyed, thorns will grow on the altars, and people will call on the mountains to cover them. Arminians see terror so great that people prefer to be buried rather than face judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the depth of despair in the face of God’s judgment. Both traditions note that Jesus uses similar words in Luke 23:30, and that they appear again in Revelation 6:16, naming these without merging them.
